diagnosis_steps: Check that the ice maker is turned on — look for an on/off switch or wire bail arm on the side of the ice maker; the arm should be in the down position.
Confirm the freezer temperature is at or below 0°F (-18°C). Warm freezer temps are the #1 cause of no ice.
Inspect the water supply line behind the refrigerator for kinks or pinches; straighten any you find.
Replace the water filter if it is older than 6 months — a clogged filter restricts water flow to the ice maker.
Test the water inlet valve for continuity with a multimeter; replace it if it reads open (no continuity).
If all the above pass, replace the ice maker assembly itself.
Check that the refrigerator is plugged in and the circuit breaker is not tripped.
Verify the temperature controls are set correctly — fresh food should be around 37°F and freezer at 0°F.
Listen for the condenser fan (at the back or bottom) — if you don't hear it, the fan motor may be faulty.
Inspect the door gaskets for tears or gaps; a poor seal lets warm air in continuously.
Check the evaporator fan in the freezer compartment — if it's not running, the compressor start relay may be faulty.
Test the compressor start relay by shaking it — a rattling noise means it has failed.
If none of the above resolves the issue, the compressor itself may need professional service.
Locate the source of the leak — check if it is from the water dispenser, the ice maker, or from under the refrigerator.
If leaking at the dispenser or ice maker: inspect the water supply line and inlet valve connections for loose fittings.
Check the drain pan under the refrigerator — if cracked or overflowing, it will drip on the floor.
Inspect the defrost drain tube in the freezer — a clogged drain will cause water to pool and leak.
If the water supply line is cracked or has a loose compression fitting, replace or tighten it.
Check the water inlet valve for cracks or a faulty seal.

Identify the type of noise: clicking usually points to the compressor start relay; buzzing to the ice maker or inlet valve; rattling to a loose drain pan or condenser fan; squealing to the evaporator fan motor.
For clicking: shake the compressor start relay — if it rattles, replace it.
For buzzing near the ice maker: the water inlet valve solenoid may be failing; test with a multimeter.
For rattling: check that the drain pan is seated properly and the condenser coils are not vibrating against anything.
For squealing or grinding: the evaporator fan motor bearings may be worn — replace the motor.
Check that the spray arms spin freely — remove them and look for clogged holes; use a toothpick to clear any blockages.
Inspect the spray arm for cracks — a cracked arm loses pressure and cannot clean effectively.
Clean the filter assembly at the bottom of the dishwasher; a clogged filter dramatically reduces cleaning.
Verify water temperature is at least 120°F — run hot water at the sink before starting the cycle.
Check the detergent dispenser opens properly during the wash cycle.
If the motor makes noise but water pressure is weak, the wash pump may be failing.
Identify where the leak originates — from the door, under the unit, or from connections at the back.
If leaking from the door: inspect the door gasket for tears, cracks, or sections that have come loose; replace if damaged.
Ensure the dishwasher is level — an unlevel unit can cause water to pool against the door and leak.
Check the door latch — if the door does not close completely, water will spray out.
If leaking from under the unit: inspect the pump hoses and water inlet connections for looseness.
Overfilling can also cause leaks — ensure the float switch inside the tub moves freely.
Confirm the dishwasher is getting power — check the circuit breaker and ensure the unit is plugged in.
Make sure the door is fully latched — dishwashers won't run unless the door latch engages the door switch.
Try a hard reset: turn off the circuit breaker for 60 seconds, then restore power.
Check for a Control Lock or Child Lock indicator on the panel — hold the lock button for 3 seconds to disable.
If the door clicks shut but the unit still won't start, the door latch assembly or door switch may be faulty.
If the control panel is unresponsive or shows an error code, the control board may have failed.
Ensure you are using rinse aid — it is essential for effective drying; refill the dispenser if empty.
Check that the heated dry option is selected — some cycles default to air-dry only.
Plastic items naturally retain water more than glass or ceramic; this is normal behavior.
Test the heating element for continuity with a multimeter — if it reads open, the element has failed.
Inspect the high-limit thermostat on the heating element — a blown thermostat will disable the heat.
If the element has continuity but still produces no heat, the control board may not be activating it.
